newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait deputies rap government over security.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait deputies rap government over security.

text.p: Kuwaiti lawmakers attacked the government over security policy on Tuesday, saying its concerns about domestic political opposition had deflected attention from guarding against former occupier Iraq since the 1991 Gulf War.

Opposition MPs accused the government of being more concerned to help pro-government candidates win parliamentary polls set for October 7, and to arrange influential state jobs for associates, than with the security of the state.

"The country is under threat and from what I hear the head of the government is occupying himself with voters," deputy Ahmad al-Khatib said in a bad-tempered debate on the government's performance during the 1990-91 Iraq crisis.
Khatib was apparently referring to Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah.

"The government,...is still concerned with pre-reserving its power and interests," said deputy Abdullah al-Naibari. "The concern of the leadership is how to get a parliament that would be obedient to it."
The government has strongly denied such accusations whenever they have been made by the opposition-dominated assembly.

Most parliamentarians' criticisms were directed at Kuwaiti security policy since the 1991 Gulf War rather than at Kuwaiti actions in the latest flare-up with Baghdad over Western-imposed no-fly zones in southern Iraq.
Opposition MPs said they feared the government was still making what they called the same mistakes it made in the crisis with Baghdad that preceded Iraq's invasion on August 2, 1990.
The government's conduct in the 1990 Gulf crisis has become a political hot potato because the assembly this year completed a critical report on Kuwait's handling of the crisis.
Some Kuwaitis argue that perhaps the invasion might not have happened if the government had managed the crisis better.

They say Kuwait should have taken Iraqi threats more seriously, but one of the reasons it did not take these precautions, they argue, was that officials' energies were devoted to curbing the influence of its domestic opponents.
Officials have explained that military mobilisation would have aggravated tensions with Iraq and anyway an outright armed encounter with Baghdad would have been "catastrophic".
"Their (government officials') concerns are focussed on positions and authority and control," said Khatib.
"We are now in a much worse position than in August 2," Khatib said. "The same faltering policies that are harmful and destructive to the country are still running," he added.
"Our...government did not benefit from the lessons of the crisis (the occupation)," said deputy Mubarak al-Duwailah. "We believe that the government is not serious about reform."
